questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have always wanted to experience Japan, so a semester abroad was the perfect opportunity!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Amazing experience! Although I would perhaps have preferred a more focused learning experience on Data Science topics (1-2 courses instead of the 5 that I enrolled in), I am very happy I could take university courses to learn about the Japanese culture and language (due to my study programme's "valgfrie valgfag" on the 5th semester).

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy, but doing your preparation from home is a must. Luckily the application process from partnering Waseda University will guide you quite far and have plenty of online resources to access regarding coming to Japan.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was lucky to get a dorm room (Hoshien Building 3, definitely recommend!), where I got assistance on getting settled and could contact a representative regarding any questions. But most information will be sent to you by e-mail/available online.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There are several orientation events you can attend, where some are more socially oriented than others.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
A lottery system for different dorms (5-20 minute walk from university campus).
If that doesn't work out, they have partnering housing providers you can also contact.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Depends on the dorm, but most dorms have a shared kitchen with personal cabinets on each floor.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Hoshien Building 3 has a private toilet in each resident's room, which is really convenient. Also has 12 floors, so if you are lucky you will get an amazing view of the city! Of all the dorm options, this is definitely the one I would recommend. It is the only Hoshien building to have a common room, where people hang out. So there is more social activity here.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not everyone was lucky enough to get a dorm room through the lottery system here. Remember to fill in and e-mail the form around the end of May/beginning of June.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: All information is available on their website. However, note that the course registration happens over three times.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Waseda official website.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very lucky! Got all the courses I applied for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Better to enroll in 1-2 extra courses that you find interesting, so if you don't get a spot on an important course, you have a back-up.
Sometimes spaces free up in the second round, so you might get an extra shot at an over-enrolled course, but I wouldn't count on it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A lot of online on-demand courses give incredible flexibility (e.g. not having physical courses Wednesday-Friday, so you can do longer trips and explore!)

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The overall teaching quality is lower than University of Copenhagen, but luckily the course load is also lower and less difficult.
Each course is worth 1-2 credits, which means you will have min. 8 simultaneous courses during a semester, which also limits the depth of each course (compared to DIKU's 2 courses at a time).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Not all professors speak English very well. They prefer lecturing or online assignments. Only the Japanese beginner language courses and a single Group Psychology course felt interactive.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I took many opportunities to travel extended weekend trips by train and plane, e.g. Hakone (near Fuji), Okinawa, Hokkaido, Hong Kong, South Korea and Philippines. These expenses are not included in the above budget, but when you are in East Asia and meet nice friends to have nice experiences and travel with, you will want to seize those opportunities!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food was less expensive than I had expected, and way more delicious!
I can walk to uni, so that is free. But travel expenses by train around town add up, even if it is still cheaper/around the price for the CPH metro. Some long-term residents get a bike, but I wouldn't recommend it for a semester, because you will be traveling alone and there are no bike lanes, so you have to bike on the sidewalk.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
A lot of clubs (called circles) for all sports you can imagine! I really enjoyed learning Judo twice a week - for free!
95% of clubs are almost only Japanese speaking, so that limits the scope if you are not trying to learn the language.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Check the Waseda Circle guide online, they have almost everything.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Experience the city, wander around, find a random small ramen shop. It will give you some of the best interactions and experiences!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Day trip to Hakone in the summer/fall is a must. Winter/Christmas trip to Hokkaido was epic. You MUST visit Kyoto and stay for a day or two while you are here, you can travel by train.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, but I am also used to traveling from having been on exchange before and I speak a bit of Japanese, which goes a long way for communication.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Hang out in the common room if you aren't busy, sign up for introduction events, join a circle, find others who also enjoy your hobbies, find new hobbies, go out and have fun!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The Japanese will often follow rules to a fault, so bending the rules is unlikely to work and will be frowned upon. Do yourself a favour and stick to the rules of queuing and public transportation, i.e. extend common courtesy. However, don't stress too much. As a foreigner, Japanese people will be more accepting and they would rather mind their own business anyways.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are really nice! Everyone is neat and orderly, and because everyone (including you) brings their trash home, the city is one of the cleanest and nicest smelling in the world, which is incredible when you realize it's the largest city in the world.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
If you're interested, get a head start and learn some basic Japanese over the summer vacation. It will get you a long way! Duolingo isn't great, but it will get you further than doing nothing!
Get an overview of your academic courses before you arrive, and make sure they don't conflict planning wise.
Embrace the experience, go with other students on day trips and to karaoke spots in town, have fun.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Enjoy the food.
Actually, the canteen is incredible! And you can get a semester-long 10% discount by joining the university COOP organization. It will cost you a small fee and you hand in a 1.500 kr. deposit, but it is well worth it if you eat there regularly. You can collect the deposit back at the end of your semester.
Also, travel card! Get a free Suica metro travel card in your Apple wallet and put like 4000 yen on it before you arrive. Then you can just tap your phone at the subway gates and on busses to travel around. Bullet trains require separate tickets and are kind of expensive.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To get to experience Japanese culture, cheap and delicious food everywhere, cheap rent 20 minutes from downtown Tokyo (!!), and to meet a lot of nice and outgoing exchange students from around the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
To keep an overview of weekly hand-ins and deadlines for 8-10 different courses at once, when you are used to focus on 2 courses :')

Their version of Absalon website has a dashboard that will show you upcoming deadlines though. Pretty convenient.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
